findings.detail: The Statement of Accounts has been identified as a priority for improvement following Internal Audit findings in 2025-26, indicating control, reporting or quality issues being addressed.

findings.headline: Fleet Operations and Maintenance identified as a significant governance issue
findings.detail: Fleet Operations and Maintenance has been categorized as a 'Significant Issue' requiring action in Pembrokeshire's 2025-26 governance review, indicating control, planning or operational efficiency concerns.
findings.matters: Fleet capital and operational spending are material for councils; significance in the governance statement suggests control or planning problems worth investigating.

findings.headline: Financial Sustainability identified as a priority for improvement
findings.detail: Pembrokeshire's Internal Audit review and governance framework assessment has identified Financial Sustainability as a priority for improvement in 2025-26. The council is implementing an action plan to address this concern, with detail provided in the appendix (not included here).
findings.matters: When a council explicitly flags financial sustainability in its governance statement, it signals concerns about long-term financial viability that directly matter to lenders evaluating creditworthiness.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget - Outturn Monitoring Report – 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing rent arrears growing despite 99% collection rate; core debtors not engaging
findings.detail: The report shows rent arrears of £2.99m at March 2026, up from £2.82m in March 2025. Crucially, the headline collection rate of 99.03% masks a problem: 'Most current tenants maintain good payment records... However, a core group of accounts with significant arrears continues to grow, with debts increasing over time.' Pre-court visits have 'achieved some success' but for non-engagers 'court proceedings will commence shortly.'
findings.matters: Growing concentration of arrears in hard-to-collect accounts signals potential write-offs and weakening HRA finances. Court action costs money and yields slowly.
findings.figures: £2.99m total arrears (up £0.17m year-on-year); 99.03% collection rate masks arrears concentration; core accounts 'growing'
findings.quote: Most current tenants maintain good payment records, reflected in a rent collection rate of 99.03%. However, a core group of accounts with significant arrears continues to grow, with debts increasing over time.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget - Outturn Monitoring Report – 2025-26
findings.headline: Funding gap for 2027-28 revised upward to £32.8m worst-case, vs £17.3m base case
findings.detail: The MTFP approved in February 2026 assumed a £17.3m funding gap in 2027-28. The council has since modelled revised assumptions for inflation (upward to 3.5%), rejected NJC pay offers (+0.3%), and likely cost-of-living pressures in social care demand. The revised worst-case pressure is £32.8m, with only £4.6m coming from council tax increase and £5m from AEF. This leaves a structural gap of £10.5m+ in required savings.
findings.matters: The council is now openly acknowledging that forward-year budgets are unbalanced without major service reductions or reserve drawdown. This is a pre-crisis position.
findings.figures: Base case gap £17.3m; revised worst-case £32.8m; funded by AEF £5m + council tax £4.6m; required savings £10.5m+
findings.quote: Potential 2027-28 Pressures 32.8 [£m]. This is assumed to represent the current worst-case scenario. A more detailed review and full update will be provided as part of the Quarter 1 2026-27 Budget Monitoring report.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget - Outturn Monitoring Report – 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery collapsed to 78%, creating financing uncertainties
findings.detail: Actual capital spending was £122.2m against a projected £157.3m (only 78% delivery). The report attributes this to 'market capacity constraints in delivering schemes and inaccuracies in profiles from project managers.' Capital slippage directly reduces borrowing requirement for 2025-26 but creates profile uncertainty for the MTFP. The council notes: 'Ongoing inflationary pressures continue to affect both materials and labour costs.'
findings.matters: Large slippage suggests weak project delivery capacity and cost estimation. It also defers borrowing needs into future years, creating timing risks for interest rate exposure.
findings.figures: £122.2m actual vs £157.3m projected (78% delivery); slippage of £35.1m; actual borrowing £35m in 2025-26 vs budgeted £86.3m
findings.quote: Delivery of capital projects is inherently complex and can extend across multiple financial years. Ongoing inflationary pressures continue to affect both materials and labour costs, which have had, and will continue to have, a detrimental impact on the delivery of the Council's ambitious capital programme.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget - Outturn Monitoring Report – 2025-26
findings.headline: Adult social care supported accommodation overspending by £1.95m despite 'preventions' agenda
findings.detail: Despite a council-wide push toward 'preventions' and cost-effective care models, supported accommodation overspent by £1.952m (improving only slightly from Q3). The overspend is driven by 'higher-than-expected demand for Learning Disability care packages and increasingly complex client needs.' The report projects: 'rising pressures expected in the medium to long term.' This is structural, not temporary.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends in adult care signal that preventions are not working at scale. Medium-term budget pressures will require either service cuts or ongoing subsidy.
findings.figures: £1.952m overspend in supported accommodation; Learning Disability and Mental Health packages showing 'increasing complexity and cost'; underspends elsewhere offset this
findings.quote: Supported Accommodation reports a £1.952m overspend, though this has reduced by £0.173m since Q3, driven by higher-than-expected demand for Learning Disability care packages and increasingly complex client needs.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget - Outturn Monitoring Report – 2025-26
findings.headline: Statutory accounts missed 30 June deadline for second year running
findings.detail: The report states: 'we will miss the 30 June 2026 statutory deadline for completion due to delays in finalising the Statement of Accounts for 2024-25.' This is a regulatory failure. Audit Wales will not clear the accounts on time, delaying governance and audit sign-off.
findings.matters: Repeated failure to meet statutory audit deadlines is a governance weakness. Lenders rely on timely audited accounts to assess council financial position.
findings.figures: 30 June 2026 deadline missed; delays cascade from 2024-25 unresolved
findings.quote: we will miss the 30 June 2026 statutory deadline for completion due to delays in finalising the Statement of Accounts for 2024-25.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget - Outturn Monitoring Report – 2025-26
findings.headline: Council Tax arrears surged 56% in a single year to £19.5m
findings.detail: Council Tax arrears rose from £12.506m (March 2025) to £19.479m (March 2026). The underlying cause is 389 properties transferred from Business Rates to Council Tax, creating £2.1m in arrears from appeals-in-progress. The council notes 'There is likely to be additional debt within this category that has not yet been quantified.' Collection recovery processes are being 'streamlined' but this is reactive, not preventive.
findings.matters: Large arrears growth indicates loss of control over a major revenue stream. The unquantified additional debt from disputed property transfers is a contingent liability.
findings.figures: £19.5m total arrears (up from £12.5m); £2.1m from second-home premiums on properties under VOA appeal; £7.306m in arrears under 1 year alone
findings.quote: Total Council Tax arrears have increased during 2025-26 to £19.5m. There is likely to be additional debt within this category that has not yet been quantified.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget - Outturn Monitoring Report – 2025-26
findings.headline: School balances collapsing, 24 schools now in deficit
findings.detail: School balances fell from £2.772m to £1.515m during 2025-26, with 24 schools (22 primary, 2 secondary) ending the year in deficit. The report explicitly warns: 'Current projections for 2026-27 suggest that increased cost pressures in excess of funding received will result in school balances continuing to reduce despite staffing structures being reviewed.' This represents a fundamental deterioration in the education service's financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Sustained school deficits signal the council cannot fund education at required standards and will require immediate intervention or revenue support. This cascades to council borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Balances halved: £2.772m (2024-25) to £1.515m (2025-26); 24 schools in deficit (up from 13 at start of year); largest decline in Primary sector
findings.quote: Current projections for 2026–27 suggest that increased cost pressures in excess of funding received will result in school balances continuing to reduce despite staffing structures being reviewed.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026 - 2056 and utilisation of second homes council tax premium for housing development and acquisitions into the HRA
findings.headline: Maintenance funding for existing housing stock reduced over next five years
findings.detail: To fund new developments and balance WHQS costs against capital constraints, council has 'had a need to reduce the funding allocation for our existing housing stock as a cumulative figure over the next 5 years of the Business Plan'.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance increases future renewal costs and could impact property condition compliance.
findings.figures: Cumulative reduction over next 5 years (specific amounts not stated)
findings.quote: there has been a need to reduce the funding allocation for our existing housing stock as a cumulative figure over the next 5 years of the Business Plan

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026 - 2056 and utilisation of second homes council tax premium for housing development and acquisitions into the HRA
findings.headline: Rent cap prevents revenue raising despite Pembrokeshire having Wales's lowest council house rents
findings.detail: Council has lowest rents of all stock-retaining authorities in Wales. New 10-year Rent and Service Charge Standard (2026-36) maintains income cap that has been in place for five years, preventing council from using typical revenue lever.
findings.matters: Council structurally disadvantaged vs other authorities and cannot use rent rises to address financial pressures.
findings.figures: Lowest rents in Wales; cap maintained through 2026-2036
findings.quote: The income cap introduced five years ago and maintained in the new 10-year Welsh Government Rent and Service Charge Standard 2026-36 makes it virtually impossible to change this position.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026 - 2056 and utilisation of second homes council tax premium for housing development and acquisitions into the HRA
findings.headline: HRA borrowing of £321.4m approaches self-imposed cap within five years
findings.detail: Plan involves £321.4m borrowing over 30 years (up from £285m in previous plan), with borrowing only £0.7m below self-imposed cap by year 5. Paper explicitly warns 'there are a number of years where the HRA account comes close to breaching its self-imposed borrowing cap' and notes this 'may require corrective action'.
findings.matters: Early approach to cap constrains financial flexibility and may force corrective action cutting new builds or maintenance.
findings.figures: £321.4m total borrowing (£285m in previous plan); £0.7m headroom to cap in year 5
findings.quote: There are a number of years where the HRA account comes close to breaching its self-imposed borrowing cap which this Authority believes is prudent and sustainable.

findings.headline: Structural demographic pressure: 85+ population projected to increase 33% by 2030; dementia cases to rise 49% by 2040
findings.detail: Pembrokeshire faces demographic headwinds that will inexorably drive social care demand upward. The 85+ population is projected to increase 33% by 2030, and dementia cases in West Wales are expected to increase 49% by 2040. These underpin the £10.1m social care pressure identified in this budget and will recur every budget cycle.
findings.matters: Demographic pressures are structural, measurable, and cannot be solved by efficiency savings or policy choices. They indicate social care costs will rise every year regardless of council actions. This is a long-term structural headwind on budget sustainability.
findings.figures: 85+ population growth 33% by 2030; dementia growth 49% by 2040
findings.quote: Pembrokeshire's 85+ population projected to increase by 33% by 2030, and the number of people living with dementia in West Wales expected to increase by 49% by 2040.

findings.headline: NJC pay spine restructuring creates £1.1m permanent increase in baseline pay costs from April 2026
findings.detail: From 1 April 2026, Spinal Column Point 2 will be permanently deleted from the NJC pay spine, creating a £0.7m permanent pressure. SCP3 may also be deleted from April 2027, adding £0.4m more. These changes permanently raise baseline pay costs for lower grades and are expected to recur.
findings.matters: Pay spine restructuring creates permanent, unfundable increases in baseline costs. These are not one-off pressures; they recur every year thereafter. The £1.1m total represents costs the council must absorb indefinitely, with no discretion to reverse.
findings.figures: £0.7m for SCP2 deletion from April 2026; £0.4m additional for potential SCP3 deletion
findings.quote: accepting that this would result in a base budget pressure of £0.7m for 2026-27. Consequentially, remodelling the Lower NJC grades has identified a further £0.4m pressure.

findings.headline: Real Living Wage increased 6.7% but council only budgeted 3.3%, creating £1.9m unbudgeted social care cost increase
findings.detail: Real Living Wage was announced on 22 October 2025 at £13.45 per hour, a 6.7% increase. The council had budgeted only 3.3% for care worker inflation. This gap creates an unbudgeted £1.9m pressure on social care provider fees for 2026-27, representing costs the council must absorb despite accurate forecasting being impossible.
findings.matters: This demonstrates that cost assumptions can be radically wrong, driven by factors outside the council's control. The council depends on external care provider inflation, which proved double the budgeted rate. This is exactly the type of cost shock that breaks budgets and forces reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: 3.3% budgeted inflation; 6.7% actual RLW increase; £1.9m unbudgeted pressure materialised
findings.quote: The RLW increase for 2026-27 was announced on 22 October 2025 at £13.45, a 6.7% increase. This is above our original budgeted assumption of 3.3%, resulting in an additional £1.9m pressure for 2026-27.

findings.headline: No contingency budget allocated for 2026-27; any unplanned pressures must be met from reserves or in-year savings
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states no contingency has been put in place for 2026-27. This means zero buffer for unexpected events. Any additional pressures during the year must be resolved by finding unexpected savings or drawing on reserves.
findings.matters: Contingency is a standard governance requirement; most councils hold 1-2% of budget as a buffer. Zero contingency is a high-risk position that leaves the council unable to respond to shocks. Given the social care market volatility and cost overruns already documented, this is particularly risky.
findings.figures: £0 contingency allocation
findings.quote: No contingency has been put in place for 2026-27. Any other additional in year financial pressures would have to be met from in year savings or reserves.

findings.headline: Projected funding gap of £14.7m for 2026-27 is identified but resolution mechanism is not demonstrated
findings.detail: Service pressures total £29.9m while funding from AEF and Council Tax base adjustment totals only £15.2m, creating a gap of £14.7m. The paper states the gap 'will need to be met through a combination of budget savings, increase in Council Tax, use of Council Tax premiums and use of reserves' but does not provide evidence in this appendix that the gap is bridgeable.
findings.matters: A £14.7m shortfall represents a material deficit (~8-9% of budget). The paper does not demonstrate that identified savings, tax increases, or reserve drawdowns can close this. Unresolved deficits force unsustainable choices or underfunded services.
findings.figures: £14.7m funding gap; £29.9m service pressures against £15.2m funding increase
findings.quote: The projected funding gap for 2026-27 based on the final AEF discussed in Appendix B and including £0.9m of additional budget growth is £14.7m

findings.headline: Council voluntarily reduced Second Homes Council Tax premium from 150% to 125%, forgoing £1.4m recurring revenue
findings.detail: On 9 October 2025, council reduced the Second Homes premium, cutting Second Homes Council Tax income from £8.372m to £6.978m. This materialises a risk explicitly flagged in prior budget papers. The same premium was reduced in 2025-26 (150% to 125%), creating a £2.3m pressure that year. This is a discretionary policy choice, not a mandatory reduction.
findings.matters: This is a self-inflicted revenue loss. The council's own papers flagged this risk in previous years but approved the reduction anyway. It suggests either insufficient financial literacy in governance or political priorities overriding financial sustainability. The pattern (two consecutive cuts) indicates the risk may recur.
findings.figures: £1.4m revenue loss in 2026-27; £2.3m loss in 2025-26 from similar decision; Second Homes income falls from £8.372m to £6.978m
findings.quote: The decision by Council on 9 October 2025 to reduce the Second Homes Premium from 150% to 125% for 2026-27 resulted in a reduction of Second Homes Council Tax income raised from £ 8.372m to £ 6.978m, a base funding reduction of £1.394m.

findings.headline: Social Care Supported Living Services overspend of £2.1m is being locked into the budget base as permanent pressure
findings.detail: Q3 2025-26 budget monitoring reported a £2.1m projected overspend in Supported Living Services due to increased demand. Rather than treating this as temporary, the council is rebasing it as a permanent £1.8m pressure for 2026-27, acknowledging that demand increases are structural and the overspend will recur.
findings.matters: Current-year overspends indicate the budget base was set incorrectly. Rebasing an overspend as permanent means the council is locked into higher baseline costs going forward. Demand-driven social care overspends are particularly serious because they cannot be solved by operational efficiency.
findings.figures: £2.1m Q3 2025-26 projected overspend; £1.8m rebased as permanent 2026-27 base pressure
findings.quote: This reports a projected overspend of £2.1m in Supported Living Services (SLS) budget in Adult Social Care resulting from increases in demand. This increase in demand is expected to be mostly permanent in nature, requiring a rebasing of the 2025-26 budget to reflect the full year cost of additional clients of £1.8m.

findings.headline: School balances projected to fall into aggregate deficit by 2027-28
findings.detail: School balances have declined from £10.721m in 2021-22 to £1.499m at end of 2025-26. Forty-seven of 61 schools are relying on existing balances to fund in-year spending, and 18 schools already operate with deficit balances. The paper's graph explicitly shows schools reaching aggregate deficit by 2027-28 if current trajectory continues.
findings.matters: School reserve depletion indicates unsustainable service delivery. Once balances exhaust, schools become dependent on central council funding, creating a structural cost pressure that feeds back into the budget. Deficit schools also signal governance failures in school-level budget management.
findings.figures: £10.721m (2021-22) declining to £1.499m (end 2025-26); 18 schools with deficit balances; 47 of 61 schools using balances to fund spending
findings.quote: School balances have declined from £10.721m in 2021-22 to a projected £1.499m at the end of 2025-26 with 18 schools operating with a deficit balance during 2025-26

findings.headline: Schools Individual School Balances transition to potential deficits by 2026-27
findings.detail: Schools ISB Balances move from £3.055m reserve (2024-25) through projected outturn of £1.499m (2025-26), then drop to zero in the estimate, followed by figures of 1,160 and 2,237 in subsequent years. The shift from parenthesised balances to unparenthesised numbers suggests a transition to deficit positions.
findings.matters: If schools budgets are moving into deficit, this signals education funding stress and would require general fund bailouts, creating pressure on council finances and reducing reserves further.
findings.figures: £3.055m (2024-25) declining through £0 (2025-26 estimate) to 1,160 and 2,237 in 2026-27 and 2027-28

findings.headline: Initiative Fund reserve depleted by 62% between 2025-26 outturn and estimate
findings.detail: The Initiative Fund shows projected outturn of £15.924m for 2025-26, but the estimate drops to £6.788m—a £9.1m reduction. The fund continues declining to £6.358m by 2028-29, leaving less than 40% of the original reserve.
findings.matters: A large drawdown of discretionary reserves indicates major one-off spending commitments or strategic reprioritisation. This substantially reduces the council's financial flexibility to manage unexpected pressures or opportunities.
findings.figures: £17.993m (2024-25 closing) to £15.924m (2025-26 outturn) then £6.788m (estimate); further declining to £6.358m by 2028-29

findings.headline: Council Tax premium reserves drawn from £12.8m to £429k by 2028-29
findings.detail: The Corporate - Earmarked use of Council Tax Premiums reserve declines from £12.793m (2024-25) to £7.671m (2025-26), then £3.201m (2026-27), eventually reaching just £429k by 2028-29. This represents near-total depletion of reserves built from council tax premiums on second homes.
findings.matters: Council tax premium reserves are earmarked funding. Rapid drawdown to near-zero suggests either the intended purpose is concluded or the council is drawing on these reserves to support underlying budget pressures, raising sustainability concerns.
findings.quote: Corporate - Earmarked use of Council Tax Premiums (12,793) (11,493) (11,493) (7,671) (3,201) (429)

findings.headline: Asset Renewal & Repair reserve cut by half in 2025-26
findings.detail: The Asset Renewal & Repair reserve drops from £18.968m (closing 2024-25) to £9.394m in 2025-26, a reduction of approximately £9.5m in a single year. The reserve then partially recovers to £14.359m by 2028-29, but remains below historical levels.
findings.matters: A 50% reduction in the asset maintenance reserve in one year indicates either a major capital programme or delayed maintenance being caught up. Either way, this significantly reduces the council's buffer for building repairs and maintenance emergencies.
findings.figures: £18.968m to £9.394m (2025-26 estimate); partial recovery to £14.359m by 2028-29

findings.headline: Affordable Housing reserve entirely depleted by 2027-28
findings.detail: The Affordable Housing reserve falls from £10.216m (closing 2024-25) to £6.508m (2025-26), then to £2.473m (2026-27), reaching zero by 2027-28. This signals the council is systematically exhausting this reserve over the MTFP period.
findings.matters: Complete depletion of the affordable housing reserve means the council will have no capacity to fund new affordable housing provision beyond 2027-28. This represents an end to an existing commitment and reduces flexibility on housing policy.
findings.figures: £10.216m (2024-25 closing) declining to £0 by 2027-28

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Key Risks (Threats and Opportunities)
findings.headline: No AEF (Annual Equivalent Funding) figures received for 2027-28 and 2028-29, creating MTFP planning uncertainty
findings.detail: Welsh Government has not provided indicative funding figures for the remainder of the MTFP period. Grant funding allocation to each Local Authority is not known until grant offers are formally received, which can occur just before or during the financial year, leaving little time for alternative service arrangements.
findings.matters: Three-year financial planning relies on assumptions for years 2-3 that may be materially wrong, creating potential for mid-year adjustments to a budget already under pressure.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: No indicative AEF funding figures have been received for the remaining term of the MTFP 2026-27 to 2028-29 with a risk that current assumptions of settlements in 2027-28 and 2028-29 may be incorrect.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Key Risks (Threats and Opportunities)
findings.headline: Borrowing cost of £650k per £10m (4.5% rate) creates 50-year revenue pressure with no reversal option
findings.detail: The council notes that capital borrowing to fund projects carries an ongoing revenue cost of £0.650m for every £10m borrowed, assuming 4.5% interest rate. This becomes a non-reversible charge on revenue budgets for up to 50 years, and any new borrowing will worsen already challenging revenue position.
findings.matters: Capital investment decision-making becomes constrained; each £10m borrowed commits £650k annually in perpetuity to service costs, reducing flexibility for other spending.
findings.figures: £0.650m per £10m borrowed (4.5% rate), over up to 50 years
findings.quote: Any borrowing required to fund capital projects will cost the Council £0.650m for every £10m borrowed (assuming a rate of interest of 4.5%). It must be noted that this will be a pressure over the period of the loan, up to 50 years, and cannot be reversed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Key Risks (Threats and Opportunities)
findings.headline: Projected 3-year MTFP funding gap of £47.7m with reliance on one-off reserve use and service reduction
findings.detail: Over the 2026-27 to 2028-29 period, the council projects a £47.7m funding gap. Current MTFP assumes only £0.4m reserve use in 2026-27 with no reserve funding in years 2-3. Plan relies on combination of Council Tax increases (4.6%, 5.0%, 7.5% per year), budget savings, reduction in service delivery and income generation.
findings.matters: A £47.7m gap over three years indicates the council faces not a cyclical but a structural sustainability challenge; the strategy of avoiding reserves in years 2-3 may be imprudent if pressures materialize.
findings.figures: £47.7m funding gap 2026-29; £0.4m reserve use planned for 2026-27 only
findings.quote: A projected funding gap of £47.7m (most likely scenario) over the period 2026-27 to 2028-29 clearly highlights that this is not a one-year challenge, with serious implications for Council service delivery over the Medium Term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Key Risks (Threats and Opportunities)
findings.headline: Budget savings track record shows 20% non-achievement, but no contingency set for 2026-27
findings.detail: Council acknowledges that historically around 20% of identified budget savings fail to materialize, and recommends £2.0m contingency be earmarked to bridge shortfalls. However, the council has decided to set no contingency for 2026-27, meaning any additional pressures must be met from in-year savings or reserves.
findings.matters: A proven 20% slippage rate on savings plans combined with zero contingency creates high risk of either reserve depletion or unplanned service cuts mid-year.
findings.figures: 20% historical non-achievement rate; £2.0m recommended contingency not provided
findings.quote: Historically around 20% of budget savings identified have not be achieved. No contingency has been put in place for 2026-27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Key Risks (Threats and Opportunities)
findings.headline: Council Tax Reduction Scheme funding gap of £3.722m annually, growing with each Council Tax increase
findings.detail: CTRS funding has been static at £244m nationally since creation; Pembrokeshire received £8.319m against a base budget of £12.041m in 2026-27. This gap increases each time Council Tax rises, as CTRS funding only grows in line with agreed Council Tax increases while eligible claimants' benefits must keep pace with the full increase.
findings.matters: This represents an annual structural funding gap that cannot be closed without either reducing discretionary spending or raising other income; it creates a ratcheting pressure on reserves.
findings.figures: £3.722m shortfall (£8.319m funding vs £12.041m budget)
findings.quote: Funding received by Pembrokeshire for 2026-27 is £8.319m, £3.722m less than the base 2026-27 budget of £12.041m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Key Risks (Threats and Opportunities)
findings.headline: Social care demand surge with 85+ population growing 33% by 2030, while market faces instability and cost pressures
findings.detail: Pembrokeshire faces both demand-side pressure (85+ population projected up 33% by 2030, dementia cases up 49% by 2040) and supply-side instability (reliance on expensive agency staff, rising provider costs, potential market failure). Welsh Government profit elimination for children's looked-after care could cause further market disruption without adequate funding.
findings.matters: This creates compounding pressure on adult and children's social care budgets with limited control over either demand or provider costs; workforce fragility means agency spend could spike beyond assumptions.
findings.figures: 85+ population +33% by 2030, dementia cases +49% by 2040
findings.quote: Pembrokeshire's 85+ population is projected to increase by 33% by 2030, and the number of people living with dementia in West Wales is expected to increase by 49% by 2040.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Key Risks (Threats and Opportunities)
findings.headline: Council Tax premium reductions creating £3.6m recurring structural pressure
findings.detail: The council has cut the second homes premium twice in succession: from 200% to 150% in 2025-26 (£2.3m pressure) and again to 125% for 2026-27 (£1.3m pressure). The risk register identifies this as a recurring risk if future policy decisions or legislative change occur.
findings.matters: These are not one-off pressures but recurring annual reductions in council tax income that are politically driven and create structural budget gaps that lenders must price into risk assessment.
findings.figures: £2.3m 2025-26 pressure, £1.3m 2026-27 pressure
findings.quote: the recent Council decision to reduce the premium to 125% for 2026-27 creating an additional £1.3m pressure on the 2026-27 Budget and a reduction in the benefit achieved from a 1% increase in Council Tax.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Key Risks (Threats and Opportunities)
findings.headline: School balances moving into aggregated deficit by 2027-28
findings.detail: Individual schools face such significant financial pressures that overall school balances are likely to become an aggregated deficit by 2027-28. The council notes this must be carefully managed to avoid knock-on impact on council financial resilience, and that licensed deficit recovery plans must be deliverable within agreed timescales.
findings.matters: School deficits represent a structural education funding crisis that will require either council subsidy or service reduction, and signals potential wider financial instability at the council.
findings.figures: Aggregated deficit expected by 2027-28
findings.quote: It is very likely that the overall balances of schools will be an aggregated deficit by 2027-28. This overall deficit balance for schools will need to be carefully managed in order to ensure that there is no knock-on impact on the Council's financial resilience.

findings.headline: Council has flagged a projected funding gap for 2026-27 and built discretion to use MRP payment holiday as contingency.
findings.detail: Pembrokeshire has identified a projected funding gap for 2026-27 that must be bridged to balance the budget. The council has included discretion in the MRP policy to use a Welsh Government flexibility allowing MRP payment holidays (repayable over up to 10 years) if unforeseen financial pressure materialises, despite flagging concerns about Wellbeing of Future Generations Act compliance.
findings.matters: Deferring MRP payments reduces immediate cash pressure but increases future liabilities. The council's preparation to use this contingency signals it expects 2026-27 budget stress. A lender needs to understand whether the gap closes through savings or indicates deeper structural problems.
findings.figures: Repayment over a period of up to ten years
findings.quote: Whilst there are no plans to utilise this new flexibility to bridge the projected funding gap and balance the budget for 2026-27, we have included it in the MRP policy for 2026-27 to give the Director of Resources discretion to utilise it if required, e.g. to mitigate an unforeseen financial pressure in 2026-27.

findings.headline: Multiple large savings dependent on Welsh Government grants that could be withdrawn
findings.detail: At least eight proposals (E4, E5, E6, E7, E11, E12, E1, S7) assume continued or increased Welsh Government grant funding or partner agency contributions. Several explicitly flag the risk: for example E7 notes 'a risk is that in future the WG grants may reduce or cease' (£162,000 saving), and E1 warns that 'if grants are reduced or stop, it could affect our ability to support schools'.
findings.matters: A material portion of the savings plan relies on external funding that the council cannot control. If WG grants reduce, the council will have to find additional cuts.
findings.figures: At least £637,000 explicitly dependent on Welsh Government grants (E1, E4, E7 plus others); likely higher when E5, E6, E11, E12, S7 are included
findings.quote: Use Welsh Government Grant to fund some Inclusion activity which is currently funded by PCC. The impact is limited but a aisk is that in future the WG grants may reduce or cease.

findings.headline: Planning team cuts to 1.6 FTE below requirement will prevent statutory duties and economic growth
findings.detail: Rank 71 cuts planning staff and explicitly warns of 'failure to deliver statutory duties, delays, customer dissatisfaction, reduced performance, increase in complaints, restriction on economic growth, housing delivery and reduce our ability to address nutrient neutrality requirements'.
findings.matters: Failure to discharge statutory planning duties is a governance risk, and restriction of housing and economic growth affects the council's long-term financial base.
findings.figures: 1.6 FTE reduction; £78,000 saving; Deep Red Green
findings.quote: Reduction in staff of the Planning Team 1.6 FTE. The impact is reduced officer capacity, failure to deliver statutory duties, delays, customer dissatisfaction, reduced performance, increase in complaints, restriction on economic growth, housing delivery and reduce our ability to address nutrient neutrality requirements for development.

findings.headline: Highways maintenance cut 5% total with explicit road safety impact
findings.detail: Two proposals (ranks 73 and 80) combine to cut highways maintenance by 5%. The council explicitly flags the impact as 'further reductions in the level of service resulting in longer response times, increased instances of surface water issues and more pot hole formation. Decrease in road safety and customer satisfaction.'
findings.matters: A deteriorating highways network is a public safety liability and affects council asset values and service delivery credibility.
findings.quote: Further reduction in Highways Maintenance Budgets by an additional 2.5% (5% in total). The impact is further reductions in the level of service resulting in longer response times, increased instances of surface water issues and more pot hole formation. Decrease in road safety and customer satisfaction.

findings.headline: Audit and GDPR compliance risk from staff loss
findings.detail: Rank 56 proposes a staffing cut that the council notes will risk 'non-compliance with UK GDPR and inaccurate responses to Subject Access Requests' and disruption to 'mail and file delivery which will disrupt service operations'.
findings.matters: GDPR non-compliance is a regulatory and reputational risk, plus a potential financial penalty.
findings.figures: £20,030 saving; Red 2 Amber
findings.quote: Loss of Member of Staff within the Audit, Risk & Information Service. The impact is delays in mail and file delivery which will disrupt service operations, while failure to delete authorised records risks non-compliance with UK GDPR and inaccurate responses to Subject Access Requests.

findings.headline: School budgets facing escalating cuts up to 5% in real terms, with high redundancy risk
findings.detail: Five parallel proposals (ranks 65-69, all Deep Red) progressively cut school budgets by 3% to 5% in real terms. The paper explicitly states that at 4% cuts 'nearly all primary schools would be in deficit or close to being in deficit' and at 5% 'high levels of redundancy in schools'.
findings.matters: This shows the council has no single affordable schools budget solution and is laying out scenarios where schools become insolvent. This is a fundamental service delivery crisis, not a discretionary saving.
findings.figures: £514,700 per year per tranche (I3-I7); cumulative £2.5m+ from school budgets alone
findings.quote: Reduce individual school budgets by 5% in real terms (i.e. 0.5% on top of exisitng 4.5%), this will still result in a cash increase from previous year. The impact is high levels of redundancy in schools.

findings.headline: Children's social care staff cuts carry risk of persistent statutory failure
findings.detail: Two separate proposals (ranks 74 and 75) to reduce children's social care staff both explicitly state the impact as 'a risk of persistent statutory failure in delivering social care services to children' and note that increased workloads worsen recruitment and retention difficulties.
findings.matters: Statutory failure in children's services triggers formal intervention. This represents a known governance risk the council is accepting.
findings.figures: £169,650 (rank 74) and £205,000 (rank 75); Deep Red Amber rating
findings.quote: Reduce staff in Social Care Children Services. The impact is a risk of persistent statutory failure in delivering social care services to children. Increased workloads exacerbate recruitment and retention difficulties.

findings.headline: Social care statutory failure risk from assessment and care management staff cuts
findings.detail: Rank 79 explicitly warns that cutting Social Worker Assessment and Care Management staffing creates a 'risk of persistent statutory failure in delivering social care services to children' and risks 'intervention by the Care Inspectorate Wales'. This is not a performance risk but a regulatory compliance risk.
findings.matters: Regulatory intervention in adult or children's social care is a serious governance matter. The council is knowingly proposing cuts that it flags as creating statutory failure risk.
findings.figures: £379,750 saving; Deep Red Amber rating (high impact, moderate delivery risk)
findings.quote: Reduction in Social Worker Assessment and Care Management staffing. The impact is not delivering assessments on time and managing caseloads, risking intervention by the Care Inspectorate Wales. Increased workloads.Statutory failure,inabillity to achive cost savings

findings.headline: Finance team cut by 3.5 staff while services face severe financial challenge
findings.detail: The council is reducing finance team staffing at the same time it explicitly acknowledges that services face 'severe financial challenge and scrutiny'. This directly undermines the council's capacity for financial control and advice during a period of deep budget stress.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that a borrower has the internal financial expertise to manage its affairs. Cutting finance staff when the budget is most under pressure is a red flag.
findings.figures: 3.5 staff from the finance team; rank 58; £148,000 saving
findings.quote: Reduction of around 3.5 staff from the finanance team. The impact is a reduction in financial advice, challenge, support and expertise to services at a time when services are facing severe financial challenge and scrutiny.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 BUDGET MTFP - MAIN REPORT - Feb Council
findings.headline: Service delivery strain from workforce reductions affecting staff survey results
findings.detail: The Head of HR notes that 'the cumulative impact on the required budget cuts on staff has been difficult, resulting in increased pressure being placed on teams to deliver services with a reduced workforce. The impact of this is reflected in the recent staff survey.' This indicates the council is hitting capacity limits in its ability to deliver services with fewer staff.
findings.matters: Declining staff morale and organisational capacity directly threaten the council's ability to maintain service quality and implement further savings, creating operational and reputational risk
findings.figures: Staff survey shows impact; specific numbers not disclosed
findings.quote: The cumulative impact on the required budget cuts on staff has been difficult, resulting in increased pressure being placed on teams to deliver services with a reduced workforce. The impact of this is reflected in the recent staff survey.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 BUDGET MTFP - MAIN REPORT - Feb Council
findings.headline: Council Tax premium policy risk materialised: second reduction creates £1.3m new pressure in year
findings.detail: The S151 Officer flagged in prior-year budget that use of Council Tax premiums to fund the budget was a risk. This year the risk was realised: Council reduced Second Homes premium from 150% (2025-26) to 125% (2026-27), creating an additional £1.3m pressure. Previous year's reduction from 200% to 150% created £2.3m pressure. Political decisions are eating into budget flexibility.
findings.matters: Council Tax premium income is politically volatile and discretionary; two successive reductions totalling £3.6m in new pressures show the council is losing control over its own revenue base and cannot rely on premium income for budget stability
findings.figures: £1.3m pressure from 2026-27 premium reduction; £2.3m from 2025-26 reduction; total £3.6m
findings.quote: This risk was realised with the Council decision to reduce the Second Homes Council Tax Premium from 200% to 150% for 2025-26 creating an additional £2.3m pressure for the 2025-26 Budget and has been realised again with the Council decision to reduce the premium to 125% for 2026-27 creating an additional £1.3m pressure on the 2026-27 Budget.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 BUDGET MTFP - MAIN REPORT - Feb Council
findings.headline: Social Care demand pressures of £30.5m over MTFP driven by learner complexity and 6.7% pay award
findings.detail: Social Care represents £12.0m of the 2026-27 service pressures (42% of total). The MTFP carries £30.5m over three years. This includes the Real Living Wage increase announced at £13.45 (6.7% increase from October 2025) and rebasing of Supported Living Services to reflect increasing numbers and complexity of learners with Additional Learning Needs.
findings.matters: Social Care demand is driven by demographic and statutory needs the council cannot reduce or defer, creating an uncontrollable cost base that will continue to widen the structural deficit
findings.figures: £12.0m 2026-27 Social Care pressure (42% of service pressures); £30.5m over MTFP; 6.7% Real Living Wage increase at £13.45
findings.quote: The most significant cost pressure for the 2026-27 budget continues to be within Social Care, with a projected total increase in pressure of £12.0m for 2026-27 representing 42.0% of the total Council Service pressures for 2026-27; and £30.5m across the remainder of the MTFP

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 BUDGET MTFP - MAIN REPORT - Feb Council
findings.headline: Corporate reserves fully depleted by end of MTFP with no replenishment plan
findings.detail: The Initiative Fund (the council's only corporate useable reserve) is projected to be fully depleted by the end of 2028-29. The S151 Officer explicitly states: 'Unless there is a clear plan to replenish, any utilisation of reserves to balance the 2026-27 budget would only be a sticking plaster and would add to the projected funding gap for 2027-28.'
findings.matters: Loss of the corporate reserve removes the council's financial buffer for unforeseen pressures and signals that future years will have no discretionary capacity to absorb shocks
findings.figures: Initiative Fund fully depleted by end of 2028-29
findings.quote: The balance of the Council's corporate useable reserve, the Initiative Fund reserve, is projected to be fully depleted by the end of the MTFP 2026-27 to 2028-29

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 BUDGET MTFP - MAIN REPORT - Feb Council
findings.headline: Three-year structural funding gap of £47.7m with no clear closure plan acknowledged by auditors
findings.detail: The council faces a projected MTFP gap of £47.7m across 2026-27 to 2028-29. Audit Wales explicitly found that 'the Council has arrangements in place to support its financial position in the short-term but lacks a longer-term plan to close its identified funding gap'. The S151 Officer notes the council is continuing to work towards a longer-term strategic approach.
findings.matters: An unplanned £47.7m structural deficit over three years indicates the council's spending model is fundamentally unaligned with revenue, raising questions about long-term financial viability and likely requiring material service reductions
findings.figures: £47.7m MTFP gap; £14.7m for 2026-27
findings.quote: the Council has arrangements in place to support its financial position in the short-term but lacks a longer-term plan to close its identified funding gap

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 BUDGET MTFP - MAIN REPORT - Feb Council
findings.headline: Schools heading to aggregate reserve deficit by 2027-28 despite budget increases
findings.detail: 47 of 61 schools are currently spending down reserves to fund in-year expenditure. The council describes this as unsustainable, with the current trajectory showing school balances moving into an aggregated deficit position by 2027-28. Individual school budgets carry £5.2m in identified savings but still receive a net budget increase.
findings.matters: School funding crisis signals the council cannot afford to fund essential education provision without drawing on capital reserves, creating near-term cash flow pressure and long-term service delivery risk
findings.figures: 47 of 61 schools; aggregate deficit projected by 2027-28; £5.2m in identified school savings
findings.quote: 47 of our 61 schools continuing to rely on their reserve balances to fund in year expenditure. This is not a sustainable position, with the current trajectory suggesting school balances will be in an aggregated deficit position by 2027-28.

findings.headline: Audit Wales Financial Sustainability Report findings remain 'still relevant'; council developing (but has not yet completed) longer-term financial sustainability strategy
findings.detail: External audit (Audit Wales) flagged sustainability concerns in its report to the 2025-26 budget. Those findings have not been resolved. The S151 officer notes the council is only 'continuing to work towards' a formal longer-term sustainability approach—i.e., it does not yet have one.
findings.matters: External audit has raised formal concerns that persist unresolved into 2026-27. Absence of a board-approved long-term sustainability strategy is a governance weakness and increases refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The findings and recommendations in the Audit Wales Financial Sustainability Report, circulated with the Budget for 2025-26, are still relevant and we are continuing to work towards having a 'longer-term strategic approach to securing the financial sustainability of the Council and closing its identified funding gap'.

findings.headline: Social Care pressures continue into 2026-27, though at lower levels than 2025-26
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags continued Social Care financial challenges as a driver of the overall funding gap. Whilst slightly lower than 2025-26, ongoing Social Care pressure is embedded in the three-year MTFP outlook.
findings.matters: Social Care is typically the largest demand-led budget line and signals an aging or increasing-need population. Ongoing pressure into 2026-27 indicates a structural, not cyclical, problem.
findings.figures: Not quantified separately in this excerpt
findings.quote: The financial challenges faced by the Council in recent years, particularly in Social Care, will continue into 2026-27 albeit not at the levels of 2025-26.

findings.headline: Second Homes Council Tax premium reduction creates cumulative £1.3m 2026-27 pressure; premium fell from 200% (2024) to 150% (2025) to 125% (2026)
findings.detail: The council has now twice reduced the Second Homes premium despite it being flagged as a risk in prior budgets. The 2025-26 reduction cost £2.3m; the 2026-27 reduction costs a further £1.3m. This shows policy decisions (not external pressures) deliberately reducing a revenue stream, unravelling prior financial planning.
findings.matters: Policy-driven revenue erosion is a red flag for lenders—it shows either Council political pressure overriding finance strategy, or lack of authority by finance management to protect budget assumptions.
findings.figures: 2025-26 pressure: £2.3m; 2026-27 pressure: £1.3m
findings.quote: This risk was realised with the Council decision to reduce the Second Homes Council Tax Premium from 200% to 150% for 2025-26 creating an additional £2.3m pressure for the 2025-26 Budget and has been realised again with the Council decision to reduce the premium to 125% for 2026-27 creating an additional £1.3m pressure on the 2026-27 Budget.

findings.headline: After a decade of annual budget savings, further savings are 'extremely challenging to deliver'; RAG ratings shown in Appendix E reveal deliverability problems
findings.detail: The council has cut budgets every year for over ten years. The S151 officer now states this approach is hitting a wall—'the budget savings are getting extremely challenging to deliver'—and the Budget Report (Appendix E, not reproduced here) contains RAG (Red-Amber-Green) ratings that flag which savings are actually achievable. This signals that the council's historical model for closing gaps is breaking down.
findings.matters: If the council cannot achieve planned savings, the £14.7m gap will widen. The explicit reference to RAG ratings suggests management itself doubts achievability of some cuts.
findings.figures: Over 10 years of annual savings; detailed RAG ratings in Appendix E of Budget Report
findings.quote: After more than a decade of making significant budget savings every year to balance the budget, the budget savings are getting extremely challenging to deliver as can be seen by the 'deliverability' RAG ratings shown at Appendix E of the Budget Report for 2026-27.

findings.headline: Corporate useable reserves (Initiative Fund) projected to be fully depleted by end of MTFP 2028-29
findings.detail: The council's only corporate reserve is forecast to run out entirely within the planning horizon. The General Fund Working Balance will be set at 3% of net expenditure (£11.0m), the minimum prudent level. The S151 officer explicitly warns that using reserves to plug the budget gap would be 'only a sticking plaster' and would worsen the 2027-28 position.
findings.matters: Exhaustion of reserves removes the council's financial buffer. Combined with the three-year funding gap, this indicates the council will have no contingency for demand shocks, interest rate changes, or capital emergencies.
findings.figures: Initiative Fund: fully depleted by end of MTFP; General Fund Working Balance: £11.0m (3% of budget)
findings.quote: The balance of the Council's corporate useable reserve, the Initiative Fund reserve, is projected to be fully depleted by the end of the MTFP 2026-27 to 2028-29 as outlined in Appendix D of the Budget Report for 2026-27.

findings.headline: Funding gap of £14.7m for 2026-27, £47.7m over three-year MTFP, described as 'unprecedented financial challenges'
findings.detail: The council faces a significant structural funding gap even with proposed Council Tax increases and budget savings. Over the three-year plan to 2028-29, the gap totals £47.7m under the 'most likely scenario'. The S151 officer states 'difficult decisions will again be required' for 2026-27 to move toward 'longer-term financial sustainability'.
findings.matters: A funding gap this large, persisting over three years and described as unprecedented, indicates the council is operating in a structural deficit that cannot be closed through routine efficiency alone—a core risk for lenders.
findings.quote: The projected funding gap for 2026-27 is £14.7m and over the MTFP 2026-27 to 2028-29 is £47.7m (most likely scenario).

findings.paper_title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy, Funding, Affordability, Prudential indicators
findings.headline: Social care demand is accelerating with high cost per placement, driving capital programme priorities
findings.detail: The council projects 45 children in residential care by end 2025-26 (versus 14 in 2019-20), with average weekly costs of £6,963. It is building new in-house capacity but notes 'a national shortage of such placements' limits alternatives. Adult social care also shows sustained market instability with loss of 80 care beds from market closures.
findings.matters: High-cost, high-demand services can create unexpected revenue pressures that may compete with debt repayment, especially if placements accelerate beyond forecast.
findings.figures: 45 children in care (vs 14 in 2019-20); £6,963 weekly cost per placement; 80 care beds lost from closures
findings.quote: Whilst the forecasted number of children in residential care is expected to reduce against the forecast in 2025-26, the numbers are still high. A projected number of 45 clients at the end of 2025-26 (against original projection of 50) is a vast contrast to 14 in 2019-20. In addition, the average weekly cost of care is £6,963 (as at Quarter 2 25-26).

findings.paper_title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy, Funding, Affordability, Prudential indicators
findings.headline: Major capital project (Milford Haven schools) requires external approval but faces funding gap
findings.detail: Milford Haven school redevelopment is described as 'the largest investment in the school estate undertaken by the Council'. Welsh Government approved the Strategic Outline Case in November 2025 with OBC due September 2026. Table 2 shows £19.3m of the additional borrowing capacity is 'required for Milford Haven Schools', indicating the council cannot fund this from existing resources.
findings.matters: A flagship multi-year project being dependent on grant approval and requiring new borrowing indicates concentration of capital risk and dependency on external funding streams.
findings.figures: £19.3m required for Milford Haven Schools within the additional borrowing capacity
findings.quote: The redevelopment of primary and secondary school provision in Milford Haven has figured in the Council's strategic plans since 2017. Cabinet in July 2025 approved the preferred option to co-locate the English medium primary and secondary school and a new Welsh medium school. This represents the largest investment in the school estate undertaken by the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy, Funding, Affordability, Prudential indicators
findings.headline: Significant financial challenges acknowledged to continue into 2026-27
findings.detail: The foreword states that 'The significant financial challenges faced by the Council over recent years have continued in 2025-26 and will continue into 2026-27.' This is stated without mitigation and sets the context for difficult decisions on revenue and capital.
findings.matters: A council under sustained financial pressure may struggle to absorb cost overruns on capital projects or unexpected revenue pressures, putting loan repayment at risk.
findings.figures: Challenges continue into 2026-27
findings.quote: The significant financial challenges faced by the Council over recent years have continued in 2025-26 and will continue into 2026-27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy, Funding, Affordability, Prudential indicators
findings.headline: Capital financing cost cap leaves only 1.15% headroom by 2027-28
findings.detail: The council approved a 5.30% cap on capital financing costs as a proportion of net revenue budget. The approved capital programme shows 4.15% by 2027-28, leaving only 1.15% capacity. Modelling shows this would restrict flexibility for additional borrowing if exceeded.
findings.matters: Limited headroom on the affordability cap constrains the council's ability to respond to new capital pressures or opportunities, and suggests the council is already near self-imposed borrowing limits.
findings.figures: 5.30% cap; 3.38% in 2025-26; 4.15% in 2027-28; capacity declining to 1.15%
findings.quote: Council on 14 December 2023 approved the use of Capital Financing Costs as a proportion of Net Revenue Budget as the new methodology for providing assurance of affordability and sustainability of the capital programme. A capping level up to a maximum of 5.30% for the General Fund was also approved

findings.paper_title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy, Funding, Affordability, Prudential indicators
findings.headline: External borrowing increasing by £199.9m over five years, creating lasting revenue pressure
findings.detail: The council plans for external borrowing to increase to £391.9m by 2029-30, an increase of £199.9m from 2024-25. Any borrowing undertaken costs £60k per annum per £1m borrowed (at 4% interest) and creates revenue pressure that is permanent over the loan period, up to 50 years. The council explicitly notes this 'will be a pressure over the period of the loan, up to 50 years, and cannot be reversed.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale and permanence of new debt obligations and their impact on the council's revenue budget at a time when the council itself describes financial challenges.
findings.figures: £391.9m by 2029-30; £199.9m increase from 2024-25; £60k per annum cost per £1m borrowed
findings.quote: External Borrowing will increase to £391.9m by 2029-30, an increase of £199.9m from 2024-25 for the current and approved capital programme.

news_drafts.headline: Statement of Accounts identified as requiring improvement
news_drafts.lead: Audit findings requiring Statement of Accounts improvements indicate control or reporting gaps; lenders depend on reliable and complete financial statements.

news_drafts.headline: Fleet Operations and Maintenance identified as a significant governance issue
news_drafts.lead: Fleet capital and operational spending are material for councils; significance in the governance statement suggests control or planning problems worth investigating.

news_drafts.headline: Financial Sustainability identified as a priority for improvement
news_drafts.lead: When a council explicitly flags financial sustainability in its governance statement, it signals concerns about long-term financial viability that directly matter to lenders evaluating creditworthiness.
